Here's the likely cause and a clean workflow to sort it out. If the audio is hard left, it's almost always because a mono mic (lav or shotgun) was fed into one channel of a stereo input on the camera or recorder, and that channel got mapped straight to the left output — not something wrong with your signal itself, just how it got routed. That matters because it means the fix is a channel operation, not an EQ or pan-knob trick, and it should happen *before* anything else so your later processing isn't working on a lopsided signal.

For proximity effect: since he's alternating between singing (probably closer/louder into the mic) and talking (more variable distance), the bass buildup will come and go rather than sit at a constant level — so a static EQ cut will either undercorrect the loud moments or thin out the quieter ones. That's why dynamic correction works better than a fixed cut.

The key sequencing point is: fix the channel/pan problem *before* running any noise reduction, since spectral tools build their noise profile from the actual channel content — doing it on a lopsided stereo image can give you an inconsistent result once you center it later.

If you tell me which app you're editing in (Premiere, Resolve, Reaper, Audition, Logic, etc.), I can give you the exact effect names and settings instead of the general version above.

speaker: Claude
chat:
Good — Ableton's stock devices cover most of this cleanly, you just need one third-party plugin for the actual noise reduction since Live doesn't ship a spectral denoiser. Here's the chain, top to bottom on the track:

1. **Utility** — set Channel Mode to "Left." This takes just the left channel and copies it to both L and R, giving you a properly centered signal instead of a phantom hard-left image. Do this first, before anything else touches the signal.

2. **EQ Eight** — set Band 1 to High Pass, around 80–100Hz, 48dB/oct slope (24dB/oct if it feels too aggressive on the guitar's low end).

3. **Multiband Dynamics** — this is your dynamic EQ for proximity effect. Set the low-band crossover around 250–300Hz and apply downward compression on that band only (moderate threshold, higher ratio) while leaving the mid/high bands untouched. It'll only clamp the bass when it actually gets boomy — singing close to the mic — and leave quieter talking alone. If you want something more "one-knob" for this, Soundtheory Gullfoss (third-party VST) is excellent at automatically taming resonant buildup like this.

4. **A denoiser plugin** — this is the one gap in Ableton's stock kit. iZotope RX (Elements or Standard) has a De-noise module that works as a VST insert and is the industry standard for exactly this job. Waves Clarity Vx is a solid, simpler alternative. If you don't want to buy a plugin, Adobe's free web-based Enhance Speech tool can clean the file externally — export the audio, process it there, reimport, though it can sound slightly processed on music/guitar. Set reduction conservatively either way; don't fully strip the outdoor tone.

5. For wind gusts specifically, Ableton's automation lanes let you ride the EQ Eight high-pass frequency up during the worst moments — a cheap, stock-only workaround if you don't have a dedicated de-wind tool.

6. **Compressor** (2:1–3:1, medium attack) to even out sung vs. spoken sections, then Ableton's stock **De-Esser** if singing introduces sibilance, and a final light **EQ Eight** pass (small bell/shelf boost around 3–5kHz) for clarity.

One thing worth double-checking once step 1 is in place: listen back and make sure the "Left" channel mode didn't just relocate a problem — if the *original* left channel itself has any phase issues or a comb-filtered sound (common with on-camera stereo mics in windy conditions), you'll hear it more clearly once centered, and that's worth fixing before you spend time on the noise reduction pass.

speaker: Claude
AI_high_level_action: Diagnosed video loss during bounce export process.

speaker: Claude
chat:
That's expected — Ableton Live only ever exports audio. Even though it can load a video file into a track for visual sync reference while you work, its bounce/export function has no video output at all; the "video" you were seeing was just a reference window, not something Live can re-render with new audio attached.

You've got two ways to get the corrected audio back onto the video:

**Fastest — remux with ffmpeg (no re-encoding, no quality loss to picture):**
```bash
ffmpeg -i original_video.mp4 -i corrected_audio.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v copy -c:a aac -shortest output.mp4
```
This takes the video stream from your original file untouched and swaps in the new audio, encoding just the audio to AAC. Fast and lossless on the video side.

**Or — back into your NLE:** if you originally cut this in Premiere, Resolve, etc., just import the bounced WAV from Live, line it up against the original clip (a transient like a guitar pluck or a clap makes syncing easy), mute/disable the old audio track, and export from there as usual.

If you don't have ffmpeg installed and don't want to mess with command line, most NLEs (including free ones like DaVinci Resolve) will do the remux for you with a simple audio-replace workflow.

chat: there's some clipping happening at louder parts, what's the the best way to deal with that distortion? Rx Declip or something else?

speaker: Claude
AI_high_level_action: Diagnosed clipping source and strategized RX De-clip application order.

speaker: Claude
chat:
RX De-clip is the right instinct, but first check what kind of clipping you're actually dealing with, because it changes the fix:

**Zoom into the waveform at those loud moments.** If the peaks are flat-topped — literally squared off at the ceiling instead of rounded — that's true digital clipping, and RX De-clip (Standard or Advanced) is genuinely the best tool for it. It doesn't just attenuate the peak, it analyzes the waveform shape around the clipped region and interpolates/reconstructs what the peak probably looked like before it got flattened. Works well on individual loud syllables or guitar hits.

**If instead it looks like a messier, jagged distortion without hard flat tops**, that's more likely the camera's mic preamp overloading before the signal was even digitized — analog saturation baked into the recording rather than a sample-level clip. RX De-clip has much less to work with here, since there's no clean "true peak" underneath to reconstruct — the distortion itself was captured as the actual waveform. In that case you're managing it rather than fixing it: a touch of dynamic EQ pulling down the harsh upper-mid harmonics that overload tends to generate, or subtle parallel saturation to mask the edge, gets you the most improvement realistically available.

A few practical notes either way:

- **Order matters** — put De-clip early in your chain, right after the Utility channel-fix step and before EQ Eight/Multiband Dynamics/denoise. Clipping generates extra harmonic content that can confuse both your dynamic EQ's detection and a spectral denoiser's noise profile if they run first.
- RX's **Repair Assistant** mode is worth trying if you're not sure how bad it is — it'll auto-detect clipping severity and suggest settings rather than you guessing thresholds manually.
- Severe, sustained clipping (many consecutive flattened samples, not just a few) is harder for any tool to fully recover — de-clip does best on brief overs, not long stretches pinned at the ceiling.

If you don't already have RX, Standard tier includes De-clip and covers this plus your earlier denoise step in one plugin, so it may be worth the single purchase rather than assembling separate tools for each problem.

This intro problem is actually two separate issues stacked on top of each other, and they need different tools — worth untangling them before you touch anything, because trying to fix both with one broad pass (like just cranking the denoiser) won't do much for either.

**The chatter/crosstalk problem** is the harder one to be honest about: separating two overlapping human voices on a single mono mic is fundamentally different from noise reduction. Spectral denoisers work by learning a *steady* noise profile (hiss, hum, wind) and subtracting it — but another person talking is just as "voice-shaped" as your main subject, so the tools can't reliably tell them apart. This is the one area where I'd manage expectations rather than promise a clean fix.

**The mic-movement problem** is much more tractable — those are usually short, transient events (bumps, cable noise, handling thumps) rather than a sustained noise floor, so they respond well to being fixed individually rather than broadly.

Quick correction before the workflow: boosting ~7k won't widen the image — since it's a truly doubled mono signal (L and R are identical, sample for sample), there's zero difference between the channels for any stereo processing to work with. EQ changes tone, not width. You could push that 7k shelf as hard as you want and it'll sound brighter, but it'll still collapse to dead-center every time, because there's no side-channel information for a widener (or your ears) to perceive as "wide." Mid-side width tools specifically manipulate the *difference* between L and R — with L=R, that difference is zero, so they've got nothing to act on either.

If you do want real width, you need something that actually decorrelates the two channels (a short modulated delay, chorus, or a widener plugin built for mono sources) rather than an EQ move. Whether that's worth doing at all for this material is worth considering too — see the note in step 5.

chat: should I use inflator or reverb?

speaker: Claude
AI_high_level_action: Weighed distinct sonic purposes before seeking clarification.

speaker: Claude
chat:
They solve different problems, and honestly the answer probably isn't "instead of" — it's "for what":

**Inflator** (the Slate Digital plugin, if that's what you mean) is a harmonic saturation/density tool — it makes things sound louder and more "present" through added harmonics rather than through a limiter squashing peaks. It's mono-compatible and doesn't add space or width; it's closer to what I meant by the Saturator suggestion earlier — a way to make a single-source mono recording feel bigger and more polished without touching the stereo image at all.

**Reverb** adds a sense of physical space, and — relevant to your last question — a stereo reverb send is actually one of the *legitimate* ways to add real width to a doubled-mono signal, since the reflections naturally differ between L and R. It solves a completely different problem than Inflator: space and dimension, not density or loudness.

Given the context — outdoor, single-mic, meant to feel like it's actually happening outside — I'd lean toward reverb being the riskier move here. Even a fairly short room/plate verb can start reading as "recorded indoors," which works against the honesty of the shot. If you use it at all, keep it very subtle (short decay, low mix, maybe just enough to soften the mono-doubled harshness) rather than reaching for it as a stylistic effect.

Inflator (or Saturator) is the safer pick for just making the mix feel a bit more finished — it won't fight the "this happened outside" quality the way reverb can. If you want both a little density *and* a touch of natural width, a very light reverb send plus a light Inflator pass on the main bus isn't contradictory — they're just doing different jobs, and using one doesn't rule out the other.

**If this goes back into the full video** (most likely, based on your earlier question) — the exact LUFS of just the song clip matters less than how it sits relative to the talking sections around it. If you master the song to hit -14 LUFS in isolation but the dialogue portions are sitting quieter at -20 or so, you'll get a jarring loudness jump right when the video cuts from talking to playing. Better approach: check what the dialogue sections are currently measuring (most DAWs/NLEs have a loudness meter — Ableton doesn't have one built in, so you'd want a metering plugin like Youlean Loudness Meter, which is free) and master the song to land close to that same short-term/integrated range, so the transition feels smooth rather than like a volume knob got bumped. Platforms like YouTube will then normalize the *whole* finished video to around -14 LUFS integrated anyway, so consistency between sections matters more than hitting an exact number on just the excerpt.

**If this excerpt is going out on its own** (a separate clip, not reinserted) — then treat it like standalone content and aim for around -14 LUFS integrated with a true peak ceiling around -1dB, which lines up with YouTube/most social platforms' normalization target.

Given the project as a whole, I'd bet you want the first approach — worth pulling up a loudness meter on the dialogue sections before you finalize the song's level.
